articles.title: New Mexico Literacy Institute by Multistudio and Design Plus Architects Set to Open in December
articles.description: The New Mexico Literacy Institute (NMLI), a 31,000-square-foot educational center designed by Multistudio in collaboration with Albuquerque-based Design Plus Architects, is scheduled to open in December 2026. Located in New Mexico, the project is a legacy initiative of Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham and is intended to provide a statewide facility for literacy education, serving learners of different ages and abilities. The design brings together educational, recreational, and community spaces, approaching literacy as a process that extends beyond conventional classroom settings.

articles.title: Europe's smart fridges are being hacked. Why?
articles.description: Europe's supermarkets are under cyber attack, with hackers targeting smart fridges and refrigeration systems. How has this happened, what impact might it have on food supply, and what else in our lives is hackable? Plus, we look at Twitter founder Jack Dorsey’s new app, BitChat, and why it’s going viral in France. And after a major security problem was discovered in one of the web's most widely used infrastructure technologies (PHP), a whole lot of websites had to be taken down and patched. Could a similar vulnerability have the power to take down the whole internet? GUESTS: Kath Albury, Professor of Media and Communication at Swinburne University of Technology, and Chief Investigator at the ARC Centre for Excellence in Automated Decision-Making and Society. Phoebe Toups Dugas, Associate Professor of Human-Centred Computing at Monash University AKA the Trans Gamer Professor. ------------ This episode was produced on the lands of the Gadigal, Burramattagal, Darug, Gundungurra, and Wurundjeri peoples. Get in touch: We'd love to hear from you! Email us at downloadthisshow@abc.net.au Find all the episodes of Download This Show on the ABC Listen App or wherever you get your podcasts.

articles.title: Managing Multiple Development Tasks Without Losing Focus
articles.description: If you're a developer, you've probably had days when your original plan goes out the window before lunchtime. You sit down intending to finish a feature. Then a bug report comes in. A teammate asks you to review a pull request. Someone needs help understanding an API response. Meanwhile, another project has an issue that needs attention. Before you know it, you're jumping between five different things. You open your code editor, check a message, investigate a bug, review a commit, and then return to the code you were working on earlier. The day has been busy, but the feature you planned to finish is still sitting there. Sound familiar? Working on multiple development tasks is part of being in a software team. The real challenge is managing those responsibilities without constantly losing your train of thought or wasting time figuring out where you left off. Let's look at why this happens and how you can make your development workflow easier to manage. 1. Why Switching Between Development Tasks Is So Difficult Writing code isn't just about remembering which files you were editing. When you're working on a feature or debugging an issue, you build up an understanding of the codebase, dependencies, requirements, previous decisions, and possible causes of a problem. All of that information becomes your working context. Now imagine you're halfway through investigating a bug when a teammate asks you to review another feature. You switch branches, look through a different implementation, and start thinking about an entirely different problem. When you return to debugging, you may have to: Open the relevant files again. Go through the error logs. Remember which approaches you've already tested. Reconstruct what happened before the interruption. Figure out what you intended to investigate next. This is the hidden cost of switching between tasks. Every interruption can require you to rebuild some of the context you had before. When it happens repeatedly, maintaining concentration becomes much harder. Of course, avoiding every interruption isn't realistic in most development teams. Bugs, code reviews, production issues, and collaboration are all part of the job. The goal is to become more deliberate about when and how you switch between tasks. 2. Stop Treating Every Task as Equally Important One common mistake is assuming that every new request needs immediate attention. But a production issue, a routine code review, a documentation update, and a new feature request don't necessarily have the same level of urgency. When everything sits together on one task list, deciding what to work on next can become confusing. A simple way to approach this is to consider the impact and urgency of each task. For example: 1. Critical production issue: Usually requires immediate attention. 2. Feature blocking another developer: Should be prioritised because someone else's work depends on it. 3. Scheduled code review: Needs to be handled according to project deadlines. 4. Routine refactoring: Can usually be planned around existing commitments. 5. Documentation improvement: Can be scheduled when it fits the team's priorities. The actual priority will depend on your project and the situation. What matters is not changing direction every time a new notification appears. Before leaving your current task, ask yourself: Does this request genuinely need immediate attention? Is another team member unable to continue without it? Can I finish my current task or reach a clear stopping point first? What happens if I deal with this later? Taking a moment to make that decision can prevent unnecessary interruptions throughout the day. 3. Group Similar Development Tasks Together Different development activities require different kinds of concentration. Writing code, investigating bugs, reviewing pull requests, and responding to project updates don't all involve the same type of thinking. Moving between them every few minutes can make it difficult to maintain momentum. Where your schedule allows, try grouping similar activities together. Morning: Focused development Work on your main feature. Resolve related technical issues. Avoid unnecessary communication interruptions. Midday: Reviews and collaboration Review pull requests. Respond to technical questions. Discuss implementation decisions with teammates. Afternoon: Testing and follow-ups Run tests. Investigate remaining issues. Update task progress. Plan the next development steps. This doesn't mean every developer needs to follow a fixed timetable. Production incidents, release deadlines, and team dependencies can change your schedule at any moment. The idea is simply to avoid switching between unrelated activities when you don't have to. 4. Leave a Context Note Before Switching Tasks Here's a small habit that can save you quite a bit of time: write down where you stopped before moving to another task. It sounds simple, but developers often rely on memory when leaving unfinished work. A few hours later, remembering exactly what you were doing can be surprisingly difficult. A useful context note should include: 1. Current progress: What have you completed? 2. Files or components: Where were you working? Problem: What are you currently investigating? 3. What you've tried: Which approaches have worked or failed? 4. Next action: What should you do when you return? Task: Fix authentication token refresh issue. Current progress: Found that the refresh request fails after the token expires. Files: authService.js and tokenMiddleware.js. What I've tried: Checked the refresh endpoint and verified the response format. Next action: Investigate how expired tokens are handled inside the middleware. When you return to the task, you have a starting point instead of having to reconstruct the entire debugging process. This is particularly useful when you're handling several projects or need to hand unfinished work over to another developer. 5. Avoid Keeping Too Many Tasks Active at Once Having several assigned tasks is normal in software development. Trying to actively work on all of them at the same time is a different story. Imagine you're working on three features: Feature A is almost complete. Feature B is waiting for an API change. Feature C has just been assigned. Instead of finishing Feature A, you keep moving between all three. Eventually, you end up with several unfinished tasks competing for your attention. A better approach is to limit how much work you're actively progressing at once. Keep one primary development task. Take on a secondary task when necessary. Keep blocked tasks visible without repeatedly switching back to them. Finish the current task or reach a clear stopping point before starting something new. This approach is closely related to work-in-progress limits used in Kanban. Limiting active work doesn't mean ignoring other responsibilities. It means reducing the number of unfinished tasks that constantly demand your attention. Sometimes, finishing fewer things at once is what helps you complete more work overall. 6. Protect Time for Deep Work Some development activities need your full attention. Debugging a complicated issue, designing an application architecture, or implementing a feature with several dependencies can be difficult when messages and meetings keep interrupting you. One way to manage this is to create dedicated focus periods. For example, set aside 60–90 minutes for a specific development task. Let your teammates know that you'll respond to non-urgent requests afterward. During that period: Close browser tabs that aren't relevant to your task. Silence notifications that don't need immediate attention. Avoid checking messages every few minutes. Work towards one clearly defined objective. If something interrupts you, make a quick note before switching tasks. Of course, developers working in production support or incident response may not have complete control over their schedules. Even then, finding smaller periods of uninterrupted work can make a difference whenever operational demands allow it. The point isn't to become unavailable to your team. It's to give complex work the concentration it needs. 7. Make Your Task Progress Visible When you're handling several development tasks, remembering every detail can become difficult. You might know exactly what you're working on, but your teammates and project manager may not have the same visibility. A shared task-tracking process can help everyone understand: What's currently being developed. Which tasks have been completed. What is waiting for code review. Which issues are blocked. Who is responsible for the next step. What needs attention next. This becomes especially important when several developers are contributing to the same project. For example, you might finish an API endpoint, but the frontend developer can't continue until the implementation has been reviewed and merged. If you don't update the task status, the rest of the team might not know whether the endpoint is complete, awaiting review, or still being worked on. Clear updates reduce unnecessary messages and make it easier to coordinate dependencies. You don't need an elaborate reporting system. A simple workflow that everyone updates consistently can provide enough visibility to keep the team aligned. 8. Build a Simple Daily Workflow The practices above don't need to be managed separately. You can bring them together into a routine that works with your development schedule. Here's one example: - Start of day: Review assigned tasks and priorities. First focus session: Work on the most important development task. -Midday: Handle code reviews, communication, and collaboration. Second focus session: Continue development or resolve blockers. -End of day: Update task status and record unfinished work. Before finishing for the day, spend five minutes answering three questions: What did I complete today? What is still unfinished or blocked? What should I work on first tomorrow? This small habit can make the next morning much easier. Instead of spending the first part of your day trying to remember where you left off, you already have a clear starting point. Your routine doesn't have to follow a rigid timetable. Adjust it according to your team's release schedule, support responsibilities, and collaboration requirements. Consistency matters more than following a perfect schedule. Final Thoughts Managing multiple development tasks doesn't mean trying to work on everything simultaneously. It's about knowing what deserves your attention, reducing unnecessary context switching, and making it easier to return to unfinished work. You won't be able to avoid every interruption. Software development involves collaboration, unexpected bugs, changing requirements, and situations that need immediate attention. But you can be more intentional about how you handle those interruptions. Prioritise meaningful work. Group similar activities together. Leave context notes. Limit the number of active tasks where possible. Protect time for focused development. Most importantly, don't judge your productivity by how many different things you touched throughout the day. Measure it by the meaningful progress you made and how consistently you moved your work towards completion. You don't need to work on everything at once. You need a workflow that helps you finish what matters.

articles.title: What is your role in your agentic setup?
articles.description: A few weeks ago I wrote about how I stopped coding and started orchestrating. Ten terminal tabs, three startups, me pressing Enter all day. Then I moved the whole setup to a Mac mini, put an orchestrator agent in charge of a pool of workers (coding agents, a design agent, a DevOps agent, an accounting agent), and went from 1 PR a day to 22. I called myself an orchestrator. Then a manager of orchestrators. Both titles felt a bit grand for what I was actually doing. With my daughter a couple of weeks away, I started re-reading my favorite book of Adler psychology, the courage to be happy. One idea stuck: the job of a parent is not to do things for the child, or to tell the child what to do all day. The job is to educate the child so that one day they can fend for themselves. I read that sentence with my phone on my knee and the orchestrator asking me for the third time that morning whether it could run a migration. And it clicked. I had the wrong job title all along. You are not a product manager. You are an educator. The industry has settled on two words for what humans do with AI agents: product manager and orchestrator. I think both are wrong, and the wrong word leads to the wrong setup. A product manager writes a ticket, hands it over, and waits for the result. That is how I used my first workers. Every task started from zero. The agent didn't know my codebase conventions, didn't know we deploy with Kamal, and didn't know I hate service objects with more than one public method. So I wrote it all in the ticket. Every. Single. Time. An orchestrator is worse. An orchestrator decides every move. That is the setup that turned me into a finger pressing Enter. The agents had no autonomy because I had given them none. I was not slow because the AI was slow; I was slow because I was the bottleneck in every decision. An educator does something different. Adler is careful with the word: a teacher transmits facts; an educator shapes a person who can live on their own. An educator spends time up front so that later the child does not need them. You explain how the world works, you let them try, you correct, and you step back a bit more each time. The goal of the educator is to become unnecessary. That is exactly what happened with my orchestrator without me noticing. It did not become useful because I gave it better tickets. It became useful because it knows how I work, what security I need, which decisions it can take alone and which ones to escalate to me. I educated it, mostly by accident. Once I saw it as education, I started doing it on purpose. Human knowledge, and AI knowledge Adler makes a distinction I found useful. There is the knowledge you learn at school (maths, history, how to read), and there is a second kind of knowledge nobody writes an exam about: the shared rules for living with other people. You stop at a red light. You don’t talk in the cinema. You bring something when you are invited to dinner. Nobody is born with this. Every generation learns it from the previous one, and a child who does not learn it cannot function in society no matter how smart they are. AI agents are in exactly that situation. The model is the smartest kid in the class. It knows Rails better than I do, it has read more Postgres documentation than any human alive. What it does not know is how to live in my house. I started calling this AI knowledge: the basic set of rules an agent needs to perform tasks and fulfill its goals inside a specific environment. Not model weights, not prompts. The equivalent of knowing where the traffic lights are. For my setup, AI knowledge looks like this: Where things live: which repo is which startup, where the Obsidian vault is, which folder is the accounting drive. How we ship: branch naming, PR size, what a green pipeline means, that nothing deploys on Friday evening Bali time. What is dangerous: which commands need a human, which tables you never touch in production, what counts as a customer-facing change. Who does what: the orchestrator dispatches, coding workers write and test, the design agent owns the UI, the DevOps agent deploys and monitors, the accounting agent does the books, I do strategy and the final say on money. What already happened: decisions from co-founder meetings, bugs we already fixed last year, features we tried and killed. None of this is in the model. All of it is in markdown files, a vault, and a handful of CLAUDE.md files that I keep adding to every time an agent does something that makes me say “no, not like that”. The test is simple. If a brand new worker spins up tomorrow, can it fend for itself in my codebase with zero instructions from me? If the answer is no, I have not finished educating it. I have just written a very long ticket. Knowledge only survives if it gets passed on Human knowledge persists for one reason: people pass it forward. My parents taught me, I will teach my daughter; she will teach hers. Nobody re-derives the rules of society from scratch every morning. Agents, by default, do exactly that. Every session starts from zero. Every worker is a newborn. Whatever a worker learned yesterday (that the test suite is flaky on the mailer specs, that the staging database has a weird extension) dies with its context window. So the second part of the educator’s job is to make sure the knowledge outlives the one who learned it. In practice, this means agents educating agents. Here is how it works in my setup: A worker finishes a task and writes what it learned into the vault: a gotcha, a decision, a convention it discovered by breaking something. The orchestrator reviews it. If it is a real rule and not a one-off, it goes into the shared AI knowledge. If it is noise, it gets dropped. The next worker that touches that area reads it before starting. I am not in that loop. That is the point. If I were the only channel through which knowledge moves between agents, I would be back to being the bottleneck, just with a nicer job title. The nice side effect: when the orchestrator stops me from building a feature we already tried and killed last year, that is not the orchestrator being smart. That is a worker from eight months ago educating a worker from today, with me doing nothing. What a well-educated agent looks like Adler says a well-educated child has two things: they can take care of themselves, and they can live in harmony with others. I have found no better definition of a good agent. 1. Self-reliance The agent can get from a task to a merged PR inside my environment without asking me anything. It knows where to look, how to run the tests, how to deploy, when to stop. The number I track for this is interruptions per task. When I started, it was 10 to 15 “allow this command?” per worker. Today the orchestrator absorbs almost all of them and escalates maybe one real decision a day to me. This is also the one that lets me close the laptop. An agent that cannot fend for itself needs a human at the keyboard. An agent that can needs a Mac mini and a UPS. 2. Harmony with the environment This is the one most people skip, and it is where agents do the most damage. A self-reliant agent with no sense of the environment is a toddler with a credit card. Very capable, very fast, zero awareness of what is around it. Harmony means three things in my setup: Not recreating what already exists. The worker checks the vault and the codebase before writing a new service, a new helper, a new landing page section. The number of duplicated utility classes I had before this rule was embarrassing. Calling the right tool when needed. If there is a connector for Gmail, use it. If there is a script that generates invoices, run it, do not re-implement it in Ruby from scratch because you can. The right tool includes other agents: a coding worker that hits an accounting question hands it to the accounting agent; it does not improvise Singapore tax law. A worker that needs a new screen asks the design agent, it does not invent its own button style. Operating in sync with everyone else. Workers run in parallel. Thirty of them on a good night. One worker rewriting the User model while another one is adding a column to it is the agent version of two kids fighting over the same toy. The orchestrator’s job is to sequence them, and each worker’s job is to check what is in flight before it starts. Self-reliance without harmony gives you fast chaos. Harmony without self-reliance gives you a polite agent that asks permission for everything. You need both, and you only get both by educating the agent, not by writing better tickets. In Summary If you take one thing from this post: stop asking “how do I write a better prompt” and start asking “what does this agent need to know to live here without me”. Your role with AI is not product manager and not orchestrator. It is an educator, in Adler’s sense: someone whose job is to become unnecessary. AI knowledge is the set of shared rules an agent needs to fend for itself in your environment. It lives in your repo and your vault, not in the model. Knowledge persists better if agents pass it to other agents instead of simple .md files. If you are the only channel, you are the bottleneck. A well-educated agent is self-reliant and in harmony with its environment. It does not rebuild what exists; it calls the right tool, and it stays in sync with the other agents. Now, let’s educate. Dani,

articles.title: VITI Field Report Part 2: Converged Security and the BIGF Break-Glass Protocol
articles.description: A VITI Science Editorial | Why traditional cybersecurity silos fail at Converged Security, and how BIGF bridges the gap between digital breaches and physical destruction. Traditional cybersecurity firms (like F-Secure or WithSecure) and traditional facility managers look at the world through isolated silos. The security vendor watches the network for malware, while the facility manager watches the hardware to ensure the lights stay on. When hackers turned supermarket freezers into "heat bombs" across Europe, both silos failed. Enterprise Automations Architect Erkki Laine argues that this is a Converged Security problem. His Business Impact Governance Framework (BIGF) bridges these worlds by making digital security directly dependent on physical Business Impact. Here are the three architectural locks BIGF uses to make infrastructure immune to physical destruction via digital means: 1. The Impact Matrix (Digital Action = Physical Consequence) A traditional firewall only checks if inbound traffic has the correct credentials. It has no concept of what the command does to the physical world. The BIGF Solution: The runtime engine links every digital command to its physical consequence. Even if a hacker has compromised admin rights, the BIGF engine evaluates: "If this command executes, will it melt 50 freezers and cause €100,000 in damages?" If yes, the framework classifies it as a high-impact anomaly and demands cryptographic multi-factor authorization, mathematically overriding the admin rights. 2. Zero-Meeting Isolation (The Autonomous Safe State) During the freezer attacks, no one reacted for hours because human operators were asleep and the manipulated alarms were silent. The BIGF Solution: BIGF monitors the system at the code level in milliseconds. When it detects an anomaly (e.g., temperatures rising unnaturally while alarms are suppressed), it doesn't wait for the morning shift or a CAB crisis meeting. It autonomously severs the controller's network connection and locks the physical hardware into a Safe State—forcing the cooling compressors to run on max defaults. The IT network might be down, but the inventory stays frozen. 3. The Physical Break-Glass Protocol If a hacker completely hijacks the digital control panel, traditional IT departments freeze because they are terrified of using compromised remote connections. The BIGF Solution: Laine’s Break-Glass Protocol allows a human physically present at the site (the store or datacenter) to literally "break the glass." This physical action injects a cryptographic key into the hardware that instantly drops all remote access and internet integrations. The hardware reverts to local, manually verified control. The business continues, and the cold chain holds, even if the digital world outside is burning. The VITI Science Verdict Traditional cybersecurity tries to prevent breaches—a strategy that eventually always fails. BIGF ensures that even when a breach happens, the attacker cannot cause physical or financial destruction, because the hard-coded laws of physics protect the business. Stop operating in silos. Explore the P = f(B × S × T) deterministic engine and Converged Security on Erkki Laine's Zenodo and GitHub profiles. just google it: big framework erkki laine

articles.title: How to Install n8n on a VPS (Docker + Free HTTPS)
articles.description: n8n is a workflow automation tool, like Zapier or Make, that you can run on your own server. Self-hosting it means no limit on workflow executions: you pay for the server, not per run, and your API keys and data stay on a machine you control. This guide sets up n8n the clean way: in Docker, behind Caddy, a small web server that gets a free HTTPS certificate automatically and renews it on its own. It takes about 15 minutes. What you need A Linux VPS with Ubuntu 24.04 (Debian 12 works the same). 2 GB RAM is enough to try n8n; for real business workflows choose 4 GB or more (see how much RAM and CPU your VPS needs). A subdomain for n8n, for example n8n.example.com, with an A record pointing to your server's IP. Not sure how? Follow how to point your domain to your VPS first. The subdomain must already point to the server, or the certificate can't be issued. A secured server. If it's brand new, do the 8 first security steps before anything else. In the commands below, replace n8n.example.com with your own subdomain. 1. Install Docker Docker's official install script adds Docker and the Compose plugin in one go: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo sh sudo usermod -aG docker $USER Log out and log back in so the second line takes effect, then check it works: docker --version docker compose version 2. Check the subdomain points to the server dig +short n8n.example.com It should print your server's IP. If it prints nothing or an old IP, wait a few minutes for DNS to update before going on. 3. Open ports 80 and 443 Caddy needs both: port 80 to prove you own the domain, and port 443 for HTTPS. sudo ufw allow 80,443/tcp sudo ufw status Note that we will not open n8n's own port, 5678. n8n is only reachable through Caddy, over HTTPS. 4. Create the n8n folder and settings mkdir ~/n8n && cd ~/n8n nano docker-compose.yml Paste this in, change the two lines with n8n.example.com, and set your time zone if you are not in India: services: restart: unless-stopped environment: - N8N_HOST=n8n.example.com - N8N_PROTOCOL=https - N8N_PORT=5678 - WEBHOOK_URL=https://n8n.example.com/ - N8N_PROXY_HOPS=1 - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Asia/Kolkata - TZ=Asia/Kolkata - NODE_ENV=production volumes: - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n ports: - "80:80" - "443:443" - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro - caddy_data:/data - caddy_config:/config n8n_data: caddy_data: caddy_config: Save with Ctrl+O, Enter, then Ctrl+X. Now create the Caddy settings, which are just three lines: nano Caddyfile n8n.example.com { reverse_proxy n8n:5678 } What the important settings do: WEBHOOK_URL: the address other apps use to call your workflows. Without it, n8n shows webhook links with localhost:5678, which nothing outside can reach. N8N_PROXY_HOPS=1: tells n8n it sits behind one proxy (Caddy), so it sees the visitor's real IP. n8n_data: a Docker volume that keeps your workflows, credentials and encryption key safe when the container is updated or recreated. 5. Start n8n docker compose up -d docker compose logs -f caddy Within a minute you should see a line saying the certificate was obtained successfully. Press Ctrl+C to leave the log. Both containers should show as running: docker compose ps Because of restart: unless-stopped, n8n starts again on its own after a reboot. 6. Create your owner account Open https://n8n.example.com in your browser. You'll see the padlock and n8n's setup screen. Create the owner account straight away, because until you do, anyone who finds the address could claim it. Use a strong password, and turn on two-factor authentication under Settings → Personal. Test it with a simple workflow: add a Schedule Trigger and a Gmail or Telegram node, run it once, and you're automating. 7. Update n8n n8n releases new versions often. Take a snapshot of your VPS first, then: cd ~/n8n docker compose pull docker image prune -f Your workflows stay in the n8n_data volume, so nothing is lost. Before a big version jump, read n8n's release notes for breaking changes. If anything misbehaves, you can roll back to the snapshot in minutes. 8. Back up your workflows Turn on automatic backups for the server. For an extra copy of n8n's data you can download anywhere, run: docker run --rm -v n8n_n8n_data:/data -v ~/backups:/backup alpine tar czf /backup/n8n-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /data . The volume name is the folder name plus _n8n_data; check yours with docker volume ls. This archive includes n8n's encryption key, and without it saved credentials can't be read on a new server, so keep the file somewhere safe and private. Common problems Problem Usual fix No certificate, browser shows an error The subdomain doesn't point to the server yet, or port 80 is closed. Check dig, ufw status and docker compose logs caddy. Webhook URLs show localhost:5678 WEBHOOK_URL is missing or misspelled. Fix it and run docker compose up -d. Times in workflows are off by 5½ hours Set GENERIC_TIMEZONE and TZ to Asia/Kolkata. n8n becomes slow or restarts The server is out of memory; check with free -h. Heavy workflows and AI agents need 4–8 GB RAM. Originally published on the Volyte blog. Prefer it ready-made? Our n8n VPS comes with n8n, the subdomain and SSL already set up.

articles.title: I Tried Learning in Public for 30 Days — the 3 Things That Actually Worked
articles.description: A month ago I decided to learn in public. The idea is simple: instead of studying quietly and showing people a finished project at the end, you post what you are learning every day, mistakes included, while you are still bad at it. I picked Python automation, a topic I knew almost nothing about, and posted one short update every day for 30 days. A screenshot, two or three sentences about what I tried, and one thing that went wrong. That was the whole format. People told me it would change everything. It changed three things. The rest was noise. 1. Strangers corrected me, fast This was the single best part, and it was not close. On day 6 I posted a script that used a loop to check if a file existed, and someone in the comments told me there was a built-in function for it. On day 11 I posted code that read a whole spreadsheet into memory, and two people explained why that breaks on big files. On day 19 I made a mistake with timezones that would have taken me hours to find alone, and a stranger spotted it in about four minutes. I counted 14 corrections across the 30 days. Fourteen times someone who knew more than me stopped me from practising a mistake. The catch: post cropped screenshots of just the code, not your whole screen. People help when helping is easy. 2. The streak kept me going on bad days I am not a disciplined person. I know this about myself. Left alone, I study for four days, skip a week, and then feel guilty enough to start over. That cycle had repeated about five times before this experiment. By day 30 I had written code on 30 consecutive days. That had never happened before. The streak did not make me talented. It made me consistent, which turned out to be the thing I was actually missing. 3. The posts became a portfolio without me trying I did not plan this part. I was not trying to build a portfolio. But after 30 days I had 30 dated posts showing a complete beginner learning automation from zero, with real code, real errors, and visible progress. When I applied for a part-time support role in week four, I linked to the thread instead of writing a cover letter about my passion for learning. The hiring manager mentioned it on the call. He said it was the first time an applicant had shown him their learning instead of just claiming it. I did not get that job, but I got to the interview stage, and for someone with no experience, that was the hard part. What flopped Not everything worked. Three things flopped clearly enough that I want to name them. First, the likes. My posts averaged about 8 likes and zero comments on most days. The corrections I described above came from maybe six people total, on six of the thirty days. If you measure learning in public by engagement, it looks like a failure. The value was concentrated in a handful of comments, not spread across the month. Second, the time cost. Writing the daily post, taking a clean screenshot, and answering comments took about 20 minutes a day on top of the actual studying. Over 30 days, that is 10 hours spent on posting instead of learning. Third, the performance feeling. Around day 12 I caught myself choosing easy topics because they made better posts. A clean little script photographs well. A confusing afternoon reading documentation does not. If you are not careful, learning in public quietly turns into performing learning, and those are not the same thing. The exact routine, so you can copy it Here is what I actually did, stripped down to the parts that mattered. Every evening, after studying, I wrote three lines in a notes file: what I tried, what worked, what went wrong. Then I took one cropped screenshot of the code, not my whole screen. Then I posted the three lines plus the screenshot, in that order, and I went to bed. Total time: 15 to 20 minutes. Once a week, on Sundays, I read back through the week's posts and wrote one line about the pattern. Week two's pattern was that I kept making the same file-path mistake. Those weekly lines were the most useful thing I wrote all month, and they took five minutes each. The honest downside Thirty days is not long enough to learn a skill. I can now write basic automation scripts, and I understand files, loops, and a handful of libraries. I am not job-ready. Anyone who tells you a month of posting makes you hireable is selling something. Would I do it again Yes, but differently. I would post three times a week instead of daily, because daily posting cost 10 hours and most days added nothing. I would keep the Sunday review, because that was the best part. Three things worked: fast corrections from strangers, a streak that kept me consistent, and a portfolio that built itself. Everything else was decoration. If you try it, optimise for those three, and let the likes take care of themselves.

articles.title: Building a Charge Page Template for a Criminal Defense Site
articles.description: If you build or maintain a website for a criminal defense firm, most of your work will end up in one template: the charge page. A typical defense site has twenty to sixty of them, one for each offense the firm handles, sometimes split by county or by first and repeat offenses. They bring in most of the search traffic and most of the calls. A good charge page template makes those pages easy for lawyers and editors to write, consistent for readers and fast on a phone. A weak one turns every new page into a custom design job. This post covers how to design the template from the content model up, with notes from the kinds of problems that show up on real law firm sites. Start with a content model, not a layout Before opening a design tool, define the fields a charge page needs. Lawyers think in terms of the charge, the possible penalties, the court process and common defenses. The CMS should reflect that so editors fill in structured fields rather than one large rich text box. A starting model might look like this: charge_page: charge_name: string # "Domestic Battery" jurisdiction: string # state or county the page covers statute_refs: list # optional citations, plain text intro: richtext # first 80-120 words, answers "what now?" penalties: richtext # reviewed by a lawyer before publish process_steps: list # arrest, arraignment, hearings defenses: richtext faq: list[question, answer] attorney: reference # lawyer who handles these cases related_charges: list[reference] last_reviewed: date The last_reviewed field matters more than it looks. Penalties and procedures change, and a visible review date helps both readers and the firm keep pages accurate. Design the first screen for a phone Most people reach a charge page from a phone, often in a stressful moment. The first screen should show the charge name as the heading, a short opening that speaks to the reader's situation and a clear way to call. Large hero images push all of that below the fold, so keep them small or leave them out. A sticky call bar at the bottom of the viewport works well on mobile. Use a real tel: link, make the tap target at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels and test that the bar does not cover form fields or the cookie banner. Keep it out of the way on desktop, where a header button usually does the job. Build sections that editors cannot break Each field in the content model should map to a section component with fixed styling. Editors choose the content, not the fonts, colors or spacing. That keeps forty charge pages looking like one site rather than forty experiments. Some practical rules: Render the FAQ from the structured list so questions use consistent heading levels. Generate the related charges block from references, not hand-typed links, so renamed pages do not leave broken links behind. Show the attorney card from the referenced bio, including photo and name, so updates in one place flow to every page. Limit rich text options to headings, lists, links and paragraphs. Navigation matters as the number of charge pages grows. This guide on building a menu for a defense firm with many practice areas covers how to group charges so visitors and crawlers can find them. Keep it fast Charge pages compete in local search, and page experience is part of what Google considers. Watch the Core Web Vitals: Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift. On law firm sites, the usual causes of trouble are oversized hero images, chat widgets that load early and block the main thread, and fonts or embeds that shift the layout as they load. Set explicit dimensions on images and embeds. Load third-party chat and tracking scripts after the main content. Self-host fonts or limit the number of weights. Test on a mid-range Android phone over a throttled connection rather than only on a fast laptop. Leave room for legal review and compliance Lawyers need to review penalty and process content before it goes live. Build a draft and review state into the CMS workflow, and record who approved each page. Attorney advertising rules vary by state, and some require disclaimers on certain pages. Add a disclaimer field or a site-wide component that can be switched on per page rather than hard-coding text. Accessibility belongs in the template too. Use proper heading order, sufficient color contrast and form labels that screen readers can announce. A person in crisis may be using assistive technology, and an inaccessible contact form loses calls. For more design ideas aimed at defense practices, see the collection of law firm website design guides. Questions developers ask about charge page templates Should each charge page have its own design? No. A shared template with structured fields keeps the site consistent and makes maintenance far easier. Variation should come from the content. How do I handle county-specific versions of the same charge? Use the same template with a jurisdiction field and require unique local content, such as the courthouse and local process, so the pages are not near-duplicates. Where should schema markup come from? Generate it from the structured fields so it stays in sync with the visible content. Only mark up what is actually on the page. SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense law firms, one firm per city. It helps them with website design, SEO for the charges they defend, visibility in AI search tools and SEO audits.

articles.title: Your Free Tier Is Not a Capacity Plan: Five Throughput Myths and a Concurrency Ramp
articles.description: A demo handles one request at a time. A launch sends ten at once. The endpoint falls over. Was the model worse today? Or did nobody measure the shape of the curve? I keep seeing the same five claims about free models and free servers. Each one sounds reasonable. Each one falls apart under a ten-minute test. I run these probes against MonkeyCode's free model access and its free server option while prototyping. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Nothing below depends on that relationship. Swap in any endpoint you control. The method is the point. Myth 1: "Latency grows linearly with concurrency" If one call takes two seconds, ten calls take twenty. Right? No. That is a queue, not a multiplier. Little's Law says concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by time in system. When arrivals outrun service capacity, waiting time stops being bounded. The curve has a knee. Left of it, latency is flat. Right of it, latency goes vertical and errors appear. You cannot read the knee in a doc page. You find it by ramping. Myth 2: "Retries add capacity" Retries feel like resilience. Under saturation they are a load multiplier. Say a third of calls fail and you retry twice. Offered load can nearly double. At the knee, that turns a brownout into an outage. A corrected model: retry only classified transient failures. Use exponential backoff with jitter. Keep a retry budget, something like ten percent of successful calls. Primary sources worth reading: AWS on backoff and jitter and the SRE book chapter on handling overload. Myth 3: "It is free, so the numbers do not matter" Free tiers make people skip measurement. "It is just a prototype." But the shape transfers. The knee moves. The existence of a knee does not. A prototype that dies at ten users teaches you nothing. A prototype with a written envelope teaches you where the queue belongs. Myth 4: "A 429 or a timeout means the service is broken" A 429 is admission control talking. It says your offered load exceeded what the server will accept. A timeout says your deadline was shorter than time to first byte. Neither one is a bug report. Both are signals to slow down, queue, or shed. Make 429 a first-class state in the client. Do not swallow it as an exception. Myth 5: "The model is the slow part" Can you prove that? Most people cannot. Split each request into a time budget: Client prep: serialize the prompt, sign the request. Connection: DNS, TCP, TLS. Time to first byte: queue wait plus prefill. Generation: first token to last token. Client parse: decode, validate, store. Without all five numbers, "the model is slow" is a guess with good manners. The artifact: a concurrency ramp Here is the probe. It is a template, not a run. I am not publishing numbers from it. Stop rule first. Stop a level when either condition fires: p95 exceeds three times the level-1 baseline. Error rate passes five percent. # ramp.py - template only. Point it at an endpoint you control. import asyncio, time import httpx URL = 'https://your-endpoint.example/v1/chat' LEVELS = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32] PER_LEVEL = 24 P95_STOP = 3.0 ERR_STOP = 0.05 async def call(client, sem, rows): async with sem: t0, ttfb = time.perf_counter(), None try: async with client.stream('POST', URL, json={'input': 'ping'}) as r: async for _ in r.aiter_bytes(): if ttfb is None: ttfb = time.perf_counter() except Exception as e: def summarize(rows, wall): lat = sorted((r['end'] - r['t0']) * 1000 for r in rows) q = lambda p: lat[min(len(lat) - 1, int(p * len(lat)))] errs = sum(1 for r in rows if not r['ok']) return {'rps': round(len(rows) / wall, 2), 'p50_ms': round(q(0.50)), 'p95_ms': round(q(0.95)), 'err': round(errs / len(rows), 3)} async def main(): async with httpx. AsyncClient(timeout=60) as client: base = None for level in LEVELS: sem, rows = asyncio. Semaphore(level), [] start = time.perf_counter() await asyncio.gather(*[call(client, sem, rows) for _ in range(PER_LEVEL)]) s = summarize(rows, time.perf_counter() - start) base = base or s['p95_ms'] print(level, s) if s['p95_ms'] > P95_STOP * base or s['err'] > ERR_STOP: print('stop: knee near level', level) break Reading the output Three fields matter more than the rest: rps tells you whether more concurrency bought throughput. p95_ms tells you where waiting started. err tells you where the server pushed back. If rps flattens while p95 climbs, you are past the knee. More concurrency is now just more waiting. The decision table Zone What you see What to do Left of the knee p95 flat, errors near zero Raise the cap slowly, keep the ramp in CI At the knee p95 jumps 2-3x Set your cap at half the knee Right of the knee p95 vertical, 429s or timeouts Queue, shed, or return a fast 503 No ramp at all no baseline You have no capacity envelope, only hope Half the knee, not the knee. Headroom is for the day your prompt gets longer. The gate you ship Now encode what you measured. Do not leave it in a notebook. # gate.py - cap below the knee you measured. import asyncio, random class Retryable(Exception): pass class Envelope: def __init__(self, knee, headroom=0.5): async def run(self, fn, *args, **kwargs): async with self.sem: for attempt in range(3): return await fn(*args, **kwargs) except Retryable: delay = (2 ** attempt) * 0.2 + random.random() * 0.2 await asyncio.sleep(delay) raise Retryable is yours to define. Map 429, 503, and connect timeouts to it. Map everything else to a hard failure. What this does not tell you The generator shares a network with the target. Measure from a second host when you can. TTFB mixes queue wait with prefill. The client cannot split them apart. A ramp is a snapshot. Provider-side changes move the knee without warning. One prompt shape is not all prompt shapes. Long prompts bend the curve down. Free tiers can change. That is a reason to re-run the ramp, not a reason to skip it. Who should not use this One-shot scripts and nightly batch jobs. Nobody is waiting on them. Teams with real load tests and SLO dashboards. Reuse those numbers instead. Anyone who cannot label synthetic traffic as synthetic. Ask first. So why ship a cap you never measured? You cannot defend a number you never took. Run one ramp. Write the knee in your README. If you are prototyping on a budget, run the same script against MonkeyCode's free model access and free server option before you commit to a paid plan. The script does not care whose endpoint answers.

articles.title: Measuring Calls and Forms Before A/B Testing a Law Firm Site
articles.description: If you build or maintain sites for criminal defense firms, someone will eventually ask you to "run an A/B test" on a charge page. Before you pick a tool, check whether the site can measure the thing the firm cares about. On most defense sites that is a phone call from a mobile visitor, and a surprising number of sites record it poorly or not at all. Testing without reliable conversion data produces confident charts about nothing. This post covers the measurement groundwork that should be in place first, with notes on the constraints that make legal sites different from ecommerce. Define the conversion with the firm, in writing Developers often default to whatever the analytics tool tracks automatically. For a defense firm that is the wrong starting point. Sit down with whoever runs intake and agree on what counts: A tap on a tel: link from a mobile device A completed contact or case review form A chat conversation that reaches a human, if the firm uses chat A call to a tracking number shown on the site Then agree on which of those count as primary. Many firms care far more about calls than forms. Write the definitions down, because six months later nobody will remember whether chat openings were included. Track tel: link taps and form submissions as events Google Optimize was shut down on September 30, 2023, so many teams now pair GA4 with a separate testing tool or run server-side experiments. Whatever you choose, the conversion events have to exist in analytics first. GA4 has a recommended event called generate_lead for form submissions. Phone taps need a custom event. A minimal version looks like this: Fire the form event only after the server confirms the submission. Firing on button click counts failed validations and double taps. Add a data attribute to each phone link so you can tell header taps from in-content taps, which matters when the test changes where the number appears. Never send what the visitor typed Google Analytics policies prohibit sending personally identifiable information, and a defense intake form collects some of the most sensitive data a website can hold: names, phone numbers, charges, arrest dates. None of it should reach analytics, a heat map tool or a session recorder. Check a few things before any test goes live. Form fields should be excluded or masked in any recording tool. URLs should not carry form values as query strings after submission. Event parameters should describe the form, never its contents. If the firm uses a third-party form service, confirm where submissions are stored and who can see them. Connect site events to calls the firm actually received A phone_tap event shows intent. It does not prove a call connected. Call tracking with dynamic number insertion can close that gap by showing a different number per source and logging calls on the provider's side. If you use it, keep the firm's main number consistent in the footer, schema markup and Google Business Profile so local search signals stay clean. The richest data lives in intake. A short field asking how the caller found the firm, plus a weekly export, lets you compare test variants on signed cases rather than raw contacts. For the form side of that work, designing an intake form a frightened caller will finish covers how many fields to ask for and how to word labels for a scared person typing on a phone. Size the test honestly Most defense charge pages see modest traffic and few conversions. Run the numbers before you promise a result. If a page produces twenty calls a month, a split test chasing a ten percent lift will take far longer than anyone will wait. With small numbers, test large changes to the first mobile screen, run variants for fixed periods and keep a change log in the repo. Before and after comparisons are weaker evidence than a true split, but they are often the only realistic option, and they are fine if you say so in the report. Keep every variant compliant Each variant is attorney advertising. If a test changes headlines, claims or disclaimers, the firm's lawyers need to approve it, and state bar advertising rules apply to every version a visitor might see. Build the approval step into your deployment process so a variant cannot ship by accident. More on testing ideas for legal sites is collected in the conversion testing library for law firm websites. Questions about conversion tracking on law firm sites Should phone taps count as conversions in GA4? Mark them as key events if the firm treats calls as its main goal. Report them separately from forms so changes in one do not hide changes in the other. Is a session recording tool safe on a defense site? Only with strict masking of every input and a review of where recordings are stored. Many firms decide the risk is not worth it. Which testing tool should I use? Pick one that works with your stack and supports server-side or flicker-free variants. The tool matters less than clean conversion data and an honest sample size. SBD Marketing works only with criminal defense firms, one firm per city. It builds websites for defense practices, handles SEO for the charges a firm defends, works on visibility in AI search tools and runs SEO audits.

articles.title: Claude config: rules and guardrails for Claude Code on .NET + Angular projects
articles.description: I work on .NET and Angular projects with Claude Code. For every new project I kept writing the same instructions again: which stack to use, how to handle Git, what Claude must never do on its own, how to ask questions. So I put all of it in one place: claude-config, a public template of rules plus a small Claude Code plugin. Repository: https://github.com/AngeloDotNet/claude-config What is in the repository Claude Code loads the files under .claude/rules/ by itself, so the rules are copied into each project and nothing is installed globally. The modules are: Module When it loads What it covers core.md always stack, tests, observability, Docker scope, interaction rules git.md branches and commits security.md authentication, secrets, input, CSP, supply chain, OWASP Top 10 2025 and ASVS 5.0 frontend.md when editing *.ts, *.html, *.css, *.scss Angular backend.md, backend-architecture.md, backend-app.md when editing C# or project files .NET docker.md Dockerfiles and Compose files containers Optional modules (email, infrastructure, feature workflow) live in .claude/rules-optional/ and are switched on only when a project needs them. The rules are written in Italian, because that is the language I work in, while code, identifiers and commit messages stay in English. You can change that to suit your own team. Rules that do most of the work A few of the rules in core.md shape almost every session: One question at a time. When Claude is unsure, it stops, asks a single question and waits for the answer before going on. It never bundles several questions together. Claude makes only local commits by default. It does not push, open pull requests, create tags or publish releases unless the project explicitly approves those operations in its CLAUDE.md, one operation at a time. Without that approval, they stay with the developer. Plan before substantial work. For features, non-trivial fixes and refactorings, Claude writes a plan file first, then executes it one step at a time, ticking each step only after build and tests. No trusting memory for fast-moving APIs. For libraries that change often, Claude checks the documentation of the installed version. Verify before declaring done. Build and tests run first, and any errors are reported as they are. The plugin: kit-config Written rules are only a suggestion, so the plugin turns the most important ones into hooks: a reminder of the one-question rule on every prompt; a check that allows only one question per AskUserQuestion call; a guard on shell commands that always blocks git init, forced pushes (git push --force and its variants), deleting remote branches, git reset --hard, git clean -f, --no-verify and forced recursive deletes. Pushes, tag creation, gh pr create/merge and gh release are blocked until the project approves them in its CLAUDE.md. Read-only commands such as git status, git log or gh pr view remain allowed; a session-start hook that gives Claude the plan and the rules to re-read; a watcher that notices when the rules in a project have changed during a session or differ from the template. Install it once per machine: claude plugin marketplace add AngeloDotNet/claude-config claude plugin install kit-config@claude-config The current version is 1.8.0. Using it in a project The documentation covers three situations: New project: copy the rules and the CLAUDE.md template, fill in the project fields, then ask Claude to start the project. Existing project without rules: use the "Git only" mode, which keeps only the core and git modules and leaves the existing code alone. Existing project with rules: bring the rules up to the latest template version. The CLAUDE.md in each project holds only what is specific to that project. Choices such as architecture, ORM, database, multi-tenancy or the ASVS level are never assumed: the template asks for them and they are recorded once. The copia-regole.bat script copies the rules and root files into a project folder and can update the rules already present. Caveats This is my own opinionated setup, not a universal standard. Some details are not yet verified against their sources, and the changelog says so openly. For example, the exact PostgreSQL row-level security syntax and passkey support in ASP.NET Core Identity on .NET 10 are marked to be checked the first time they are used. Treat the rules as a starting point and adapt them to your projects. Links Documentation: http://docs-claude-config.aepserver.it/ License: MIT If you try it on a real project, I would like to hear what breaks first.

articles.title: Day 3 never came. My son and I stopped racing and built a game engine.
articles.description: In March, my son and I made a bet. 80 days. Build real software. Sell it. Father vs son, shipping every day. Day 2 ended with four words: Something has to change. Then the posts stopped. Here's why. The race stopped We'd been racing each other. Breadth against depth. Me knocking on more doors, him polishing one thing until it shone. Then we noticed something. We have different skills, and we think in different ways. What one of us lacks, the other brings. And we'd both been making games and game engines for years. Separately. So we stopped racing and started building together. Day 2 said we had to work smarter. This was it. Synergy turned out to be real. What we built Myth Engine. Myth Engine is a game engine for 2D and 3D games. The games you make can run on the web, on desktop and on mobile. It's built with JavaScript and Babylon.js, and it uses ECS (entity component system), which makes putting a game together feel intuitive and helps games run fast. You make games in the editor on Windows, with Visual Logic blocks, JavaScript, or both. The editor draws your level with the game's own runtime, so you see it as it will look in the game. And games to go with it We didn't just build the engine. We made games with it. 2D and 3D games, shooters, puzzles, platformers, worlds made of blocks and science labs, all made in Myth Engine. Inside the editor 2D Move, rotate and scale with the handles or the G, R and S keys. Split screen, minimaps and cameras that follow the player, with no code. Tile maps on square, isometric and hex grids. 3D Blender's axes and keys: Z is up, and G, R and S move, rotate and scale. Scenes built from sculpted terrain, grass, water and lights. Havok physics makes objects fall, collide and tumble. Objects built from components Every object is built from components that you add and tune. The same Object Editor builds 2D and 3D objects. Game rules: blocks, code, or both Game rules are Visual Logic blocks you connect: when something happens, such as a button press, do something. Build a behavior once and attach it to as many objects as you like. Pause the game right before any block runs, step through it, and watch each object's values change. JavaScript works instead of blocks or alongside them, with suggestions for your project's own objects and sounds as you type. JavaScript libraries can be added from a catalog, and they're bundled into your game. Pixel art Paint layered art directly into your game. Mirrored drawing, crisp pixel rotation and patterned gradients. Recolor a sprite by changing its palette. Looks and effects Ready-made looks, from old film and Game Boy to thermal camera and comic-book print. Up to four can be combined. Build new looks from connected blocks, or write them as code. Particle effects in 2D and 3D, starting from presets such as fire, rain and confetti. Worlds made of blocks Generated worlds with hills, caves, ores and trees, and a map preview before you play. Block worlds can be built by hand too. Sharing your game Web games export as a single file or a web folder. Desktop and mobile exports are projects you finish building yourself. Multiplayer is built in, with a lobby and a relay server you host. There's more in the full tour on itch.io: What Myth Engine can do. articles.title: Quote and contract from the same numbers: a wedding vendor's spreadsheet + the 11 clauses that hold up
articles.description: Every wedding vendor I have talked to has the same story. Somewhere around booking number twenty, a client cancels six weeks out, asks for the deposit back, and the vendor realises the "contract" was a WhatsApp message that said "ok booked!". The second-most-common story is the quote that got sent as a photo of a notes app, with one line item missing, and the argument that followed on the wedding day. Both problems have the same fix: a quote and a contract that come from the same numbers. Here is the structure I use, with the spreadsheet logic that keeps the two in sync. Start with one settings sheet The mistake most vendors make is writing percentages in three places: the quote says "30% deposit", the contract says "40% second payment", and the payment reminder you send says something else. Put every rule in one place and let everything reference it: Setting Example Deposit (retainer) 30% Second payment 40%, due 30 days before Final balance = 100% − deposit − second Quote validity 14 days Reschedule fee 10% of contract Late fee 0.1% per day, capped at 5% The final-balance cell is a formula, not a number, so it can never fail to add up. A one-line check next to it (=IF(ROUND(dep+second+final,4)=1,"OK","CHECK")) catches the day you change the deposit and forget the rest. The quote: codes, not retyping A pricelist with a short code per item (PKG-03, ADD-06) means the quote sheet needs only two inputs per line: code and quantity. Name, unit and price come from a lookup: =IFERROR(INDEX(Pricelist!$C$5:$C$64, MATCH(A13, Pricelist!$A$5:$A$64, 0)), "CODE NOT FOUND") INDEX/MATCH rather than XLOOKUP because clients open your PDF, but you might open the sheet in Google Sheets, LibreOffice or an older Excel, and all of them evaluate this one. A COUNTIF on the code column flags duplicates before they bite. The totals block then reads Subtotal → Discount → Tax (only if a Yes/No setting says you collect it) → Total → Deposit to book → Remaining balance. The deposit line is =ROUND(Total * Setup! Deposit, 2) — the same cell the contract will quote. Due dates from the event date Payment schedules fail because due dates are typed by hand. Compute them: Second payment due = EventDate − Setup! DaysBeforeSecond Final balance due = EventDate − Setup! DaysBeforeFinal Status = IF(paid >= due_amount, "PAID", IF(TODAY() > due_date, "OVERDUE", IF(paid > 0, "PARTIAL", "DUE"))) Add a late-fee estimate that is capped (MIN(overdue × rate × days, overdue × 5%)). A fee without a cap looks predatory in a dispute; a capped one is the number a mediator will accept. The 11 clauses the contract needs The clause list that has held up for the vendors I have worked with, in order: Scope — the exact line items from the quote, by code, and a sentence saying anything not listed is not included. Date, venue, timeline — plus a deadline for the client's final run of show. This is the clause that saves you when "we moved the first dance" becomes "you missed the first dance". Fees and payment — the instalment table, the account, who pays transfer fees, and that the date is not reserved until the deposit lands. Cancellation and rescheduling — deposit non-refundable, one reschedule for a fee, new date within 12 months. Force majeure — obligations suspended, new date without a reschedule fee, sunk costs not refunded. Deliverables, delivery, revisions — counts, formats, turnaround in business days, number of revision rounds, and a deadline for the client to pick album photos. Copyright and portfolio use — copyright stays with you, client gets a personal-use licence, an explicit opt-out for social posting. Obligations of each side — crew meals, vendor passes, travel for destination events, your right to substitute crew. Liability cap — total liability limited to what was paid. Standard in creative services. Dispute resolution and governing law — negotiation first, then your local courts or mediation. General — amendments in writing (email counts), e-signatures valid, exhibits listed. Then a one-page delivery and acceptance record. The signature on it starts the revision clock, which closes the "I only just looked at the gallery" conversation nine months later. One habit that matters more than the template Walk the client through the checklist before sending the contract. Twenty clauses, two minutes on a call or a voice note. Clients sign faster when nothing in the document surprises them, and the vendors who do this report almost no disputes — not because the contract is tougher, but because expectations were set when everyone was still happy. If you would rather not build this yourself, I packaged the workbook (7 sheets, 450+ formulas, zero macros) and the 11-section agreement as the Wedding Vendor Contract & Quotation Pack 2026 — English edition ($14, Excel + Word, works in Google Sheets/Docs). There is also an Indonesian-language edition with local tax and stamp-duty wording.
